/itineraryStops/2/smartNotes/tip.source_en: Bring 500-KRW coins for the binoculars (no change machine inside the observatory itself). Visit on a clear-weather forecast day — fog or haze removes most of the educational view. Tour groups typically allocate only 15-20 min — budget for binoculars first, then exhibits.

/itineraryStops/2/smartNotes/facilities.source_en: Observatory cafe (coffee + light snacks) inside the new building. Orientation film in the indoor amphitheatre.

/itineraryStops/2/whyOnRoute.source_en: After the dense underground 3rd Tunnel experience, ⟦G0⟧ provides the broad horizon view that contextualizes the divided peninsula geography — the Kim Il-sung Statue and Kijong-dong village visible only kilometers away. The new 2024 building also gives the day its primary indoor warming-up stop in winter and shaded rest stop in summer. The 2024 rebuild deliberately added indoor capacity to handle larger group volumes and weather-resilient briefings — an upgrade your driver-guide can use to compress the day's heavy security-and-history content into a single 30-minute amphitheatre session before walking to the photo-permitted south-facing windows. Since the rooftop closure in October 2024, the binocular line is shorter than in pre-2024 years, which actually improves the per-guest viewing window despite the reduced total deck access — a private-charter advantage when traveling with seniors or guests sensitive to crowd density.

/itineraryStops/2/convenience/parking.source_en: Tour buses only; DMZ Civilian Control Line restricts private vehicles

/itineraryStops/2/description.source_en:
Atop Mount Dora (Dorasan) on the South Korean side of the 38th parallel, ⟦G1⟧ is the closest of South Korea's DMZ observatories to Panmunjom. First opened to the public in January 1987 (replacing the ⟦G2⟧ Observation Post) and rebuilt as a three-story structure in 2024 with indoor amphitheatre, cafe, and restrooms, the observatory looks across the DMZ at: Kaesong (North Korea — historic capital of the Goryeo Dynasty 918-1392), ⟦G0⟧ in Kaesong, the propaganda village of Kijong-dong (built in the 1950s to display North Korean prosperity to South Korean observers; widely understood to be largely uninhabited), the South Korean Daeseong-dong village inside the DMZ, the Kim Il-sung Statue, the Geumamgol Cooperation Farm, the Kaesong Industrial Complex (closed since 2016), and the towering Reunification Flagpole. 

High-zoom telescopes mounted at the windows operate on 500-KRW coins; on clear-weather days, visibility extends deep into Kaesong. Note: as of early 2026, photography from the observatory toward the North is strictly restricted — soldiers enforce 'photo lines' designating where cameras may and may not be aimed. 

The third-floor outdoor deck has been periodically closed since 2024 due to inter-Korean tensions, with visitors potentially limited to indoor binocular viewing through windows. 

The new 2024 building added **indoor photo-permitted zones** beyond the sensitive north-facing first and second floors, and the cafe + restrooms make ⟦G1⟧ the day's most reliable indoor warming-up point in winter (Paju winter lows -10°C to -15°C with strong DMZ winds). 

**Operating hours**: closed Mondays; otherwise operates within the DMZ Peace Tour shuttle program (B Course: Imjingak → Heo-jun Tomb → Haemaruchon → 3rd Tunnel → ⟦G1⟧ → Imjingak, ~3.5 hours total).
